questions.question: How did the study define the long- and short-CTO groups?

options.A: Long was ≥30 mm and short was <30 mm.
options.B: Long was >30 mm and short was ≤30 mm.
options.C: Long was ≥20 mm and short was <20 mm.
options.D: Long was ≥40 mm and short was <40 mm.

questions.rationale: The lesion-length cutoff is explicitly defined as 30 mm, with equality included in long CTO.
questions.evidence_quote: Patients were divided into two groups according to the lesion length of the target vessel; The long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30mm) and The short CTO group (angiographic lesion length<30mm).

questions.question: What were the group sizes among the 235 successfully treated patients?
questions.rationale: The paper reports 159 patients with lesions at least 30 mm and 76 below that threshold.
questions.evidence_quote: In the present study, a total of 235CTO patients underwent PCI using DES were enrolled from November 2004 to October 2010.Theywere divided into two groups according to the lesion length of the CTO (long CTO group, ≥ 30mm: n=159, short CTO group, < 30mm: n=76).

questions.question: Which 2-year endpoint differed significantly, and what pattern accounted for the excess?

options.A: Repeat PCI was higher in long CTO (18.8% vs 7.8%), predominantly due to TVR.
options.B: Death was higher in long CTO (18.8% vs 7.8%), predominantly cardiac.
options.C: MI was higher in short CTO (18.8% vs 7.8%), predominantly non-TVR.
options.D: MACE was higher in long CTO (21.3% vs 13.1%) with p<0.05.

questions.rationale: Repeat PCI and mainly target-vessel revascularization were more common in the longer-lesion group; composite MACE was not statistically different.
questions.evidence_quote: The incidence of adverse clinical events including total death (3.1%, 5.2%, p = 0.43), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p = 0.45), MI (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p = 0.71) and MACE (21.3% vs. 13.1%, p = 0.13) was not different between the two groups. However, the incidence of repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p < 0.05), predominantly TVR (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p < 0.05) was higher in the long CTO group.

questions.question: What adjusted association did long CTO have with repeat PCI?
questions.rationale: The abstract gives the multivariable odds ratio, confidence interval, and p-value for repeat PCI.
questions.evidence_quote: In multivariate analysis, long CTO was an important predictor for repeat PCI (OR;4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006).

questions.question: What proportion of each group contributed 6–12-month angiographic follow-up?
questions.rationale: Angiographic follow-up was available for only a subset in both groups, with similar capture rates.
questions.evidence_quote: The data of angiographic follow-up at 6-12 months was obtained in 99 of 159 patients (62%) with the long CTO group and 45 of 76 patients (59%) with the short CTO group (Table 5 ).

questions.question: Which angiographic comparison was numerically different but not statistically significant?

options.A: Binary restenosis was 19.1% vs 8.8% (p=0.12), long vs short.
options.B: ISR was 19.1% vs 8.8% (p=0.12), short vs long.
options.C: Late loss was 19.1% vs 8.8% (p=0.12), long vs short.
options.D: Binary restenosis was 33.3% vs 26.6% (p=0.42), long vs short.

questions.rationale: Binary restenosis trended higher in long CTO, but the comparison did not reach the prespecified significance threshold.
questions.evidence_quote:
In Angiographic outcomes were not different between two groups including the incidence of ISR (33.3% vs.
26.6%, p = 0.42), binary restenosis (19.1% cs. 8.8%, p = 0.12) and LL (0.65 ± 0.82 mm vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm, p = 0.13).

questions.question: What procedural complication was more frequent for long lesions despite otherwise similar in-hospital outcomes?
questions.rationale: The authors specifically identify more intimal dissection in the long CTO group while describing other in-hospital outcomes as similar.
questions.evidence_quote: Procedural and In-hospital complications were similar between the two groups except the incidence of significant intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group, suggesting more complex and aggressive recanalization procedure (Table 2 ).

questions.question: Why did the authors caution that similar angiographic results did not establish equivalence?

options.A: Angiography was not routine and follow-up numbers were small, limiting power to detect differences.
options.B: The study randomized too many participants, obscuring effects.
options.C: All participants underwent angiography, but measurement was unblinded.
options.D: The endpoint was assessed only after ten years.

questions.rationale: Incomplete, symptom/discretion-driven imaging and small sample size meant the analysis lacked strong power to rule out angiographic differences.
questions.evidence_quote: Second, follow-up coronary angiography was not routinely performed in all patients. We decided follow-up angiography mainly depends on ischemic symptoms or by physician's discretion regardless of patient's symptoms. Well developed collaterals and myocardial viability could influence the ischemic symptoms. So we could not avoid some confounders. Third, the sample size was relatively small, and although we could not find the differences in angiographic outcomes between two groups, the study did not have strong power to prove a difference in angiographic events.

questions.question: Which treatment-era imbalance complicated interpretation of long-versus-short lesion outcomes?

options.A: Newer-generation DES were more common in short CTO, while first-generation stents were more common in long CTO.
options.B: Bare-metal stents were used only in short CTO.
options.C: No DES were used in the long CTO group.
options.D: Newer-generation DES were more common in long CTO, while paclitaxel stents were restricted to short CTO.

questions.rationale: Stent generation differed between groups and could confound outcome comparisons despite statistical adjustment.
questions.evidence_quote: Also, use of newer generation DES was dominant in the short CTO group and paclitaxel-eluting stent was frequently used in the long CTO group.

questions.question: How was CTO defined for enrollment?

options.A: TIMI flow grade 0 complete obstruction estimated to persist for at least 3 months.
options.B: TIMI flow grade 1 obstruction for at least 1 month.
options.C: Any stenosis greater than 50% with symptoms.
options.D: A complete obstruction present for at least 6 months, regardless of TIMI flow.

questions.rationale: Eligibility required a complete TIMI-0 obstruction with an estimated duration of three months or more.
questions.evidence_quote: The definition of CTO was a complete coronary obstruction with Thrombolysis In Myocardial Infarction (TIMI)flow grade 0 with an estimated duration ≥3 months with or without visible collateral flow
